title: Pendellösung length-scale neutron and X-ray interferometry
authors: Owen Lailey, Alexandre Boutot, David G. Cory, Joseph P. Cotter, Vishal Dhamgaye, Tao Hong, Michael G. Huber, Young-June Kim, Winfried Kockelmann, Jeremy W. Paster, Dusan Sarenac, Kawal Sawhney, Naume Shentevski, Ivar Taminiau, Dmitry A. Pushin
abstract: Neutron and X-ray perfect-crystal interferometers (PCIs) are powerful platforms for studies of fundamental physics and phase-contrast imaging. Further enhancing several PCI capabilities requires reducing crystal blade thickness to the micron scale, which minimizes dynamical-diffraction image blur, permits operation in the pendellösung regime where blade thickness controls beam splitting, and reduces absorption for simultaneous neutron and X-ray operation. However, fabricating multiple crystal blades with identical micrometer-scale thicknesses over centimeter-scale areas remains a major challenge. Here, using a non-etching sub-micron fabrication technique, we demonstrate silicon triple-Laue interferometers with equal-blade-thicknesses of 110 $μ$m and 350 $μ$m, operated with both neutrons and X-rays. These devices are the thinnest PCIs realized to date, enabling a factor-of-six reduction in dynamical-diffraction beam spreading for improved phase-contrast imaging, while reaching the single pendellösung length regime in which crystal thickness provides an experimentally accessible control parameter for engineered quantum-optical beam splitting of plane-wave inputs. These results motivate multi-blade PCI designs utilizing identical half-pendellösung crystal lamellae that are proposed for neutron spin--orbit and electric dipole moment measurements.
summary: This paper reports the fabrication of record-thin neutron and X-ray perfect-crystal interferometers using advanced sub-micron techniques. By achieving thicknesses comparable to the pendellösung length, the researchers demonstrated precise control over quantum beam splitting. These devices are crucial for next-generation phase-contrast imaging and fundamental measurements like spin-orbit interactions.
main_problem: The primary challenge is fabricating multiple crystal blades with identical micrometer-scale thicknesses over centimeter-scale areas to enhance neutron and X-ray perfect-crystal interferometers (PCIs).
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated the thinnest equal-blade-thickness LLL interferometers to date ($t = 110 \mu	ext{m}$), enabling operation in the single pendellösung length regime.
method: They utilized a non-etching sub-micron fabrication technique to create the interferometers and measured beam splitting and contrast using phase-flag rotation scans and limited-measurement approaches.
model_or_system: The system involves neutron and X-ray perfect-crystal interferometers (PCIs), specifically triple-Laue interferometers, where the crystal thickness controls the beam splitting in the pendellösung regime.
key_observables: Interferometric contrast ($C$ or $C_\pi$), dynamical-diffraction beam spreading, and the ability to control beam splitting via crystal thickness.
important_parameters: Blade thicknesses ($110 \mu	ext{m}, 350 \mu	ext{m}$), the pendellösung length scale ($\Delta H$), and the achievable contrast values (up to $92\%$ under ideal conditions).
main_assumptions: Achievable contrast is limited by crystal imperfections, strain, roughness, and environmental noise (vibration/temperature drift).
figures_summary: Figures show the evolution of the interferometers, setups using phase flags, and maps of X-ray interference fringes illustrating contrast measurements.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the need for thinner PCIs, detailing the fabrication success, demonstrating the physics in the pendellösung regime, and finally discussing the measurement techniques and limitations imposed by environmental noise.
why_interesting: The work directly addresses the engineering of quantum-optical beam splitting using crystal thickness as a tunable parameter, which is highly relevant to advanced quantum optics and matter-wave interferometry.

FIG. 2. (a) Schematic of the experimental setup for thin-blade neutron and X-ray interferometry. Neutrons/X-rays from an upstream slit are incident on the first interferometer blade of thickness t. A phase flag positioned between the first and second blades controls the relative phase between the two interfering paths. The O- and H-beam intensity profiles are independently recorded by a position-sensitive detector; the inset displays experimental X-ray interference fringes obtained using the t = 110 µm (PCI110) blade interferometer. (b) The t = 350 µm interferometer (PCI350) at the Diamond B16 beamline, mounted on an optical breadboard. A phase flag is mounted above the interferometer.
